summary: Alf Sommerfelt was a linguist who founded the Norwegian Association for Linguistics in 1924. He served as a professor of linguistics at the University of Oslo from 1931 to 1962 and taught André Padoux.

Linguist and Indologist Alf Torp studied at the University of Oslo (M.A.) under Sophus Bugge and Leipzig (Ph.D.) under Ernst Windisch and Georg Curtius. He was Professor eo. for Sanskrit and Comparative Linguistics at Oslo from 1894 to 1914.

Alfons Fürst, a scholar of religious studies and history/archaeology, studied at Regensburg and Tübingen under Richard von Garbe. He held a position at Bamberg (~2001–2002) and became a professor at the University of Münster in 2000.

Linguist and Indologist Alfons Hilka studied at Berlin, Poitiers, and Breslau under Adolf Tobler, Carl Appel, and Alfred Hillebrandt. He held posts at Breslau, Bonn, and Greifswald before becoming a professor at Göttingen in 1921.

Alfons Klaus Weidert worked in linguistics and Tibetology. He completed his Ph.D. at Heidelberg University by 1971, held a research position at the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (~1979–1984), and served as PD at Kiel University in 1982.

Linguist and Indologist Alfons Nehring studied at Berlin and Breslau under Otto Schrader. He taught at Breslau, Marquette, and Fordham, and served as ordinary professor at Würzburg from 1930 and again from 1952 to 1958.

Alfons Väth was a historian and Indologist who founded St. Xavier's College, Mumbai, in 1913, where he taught English and Indian history (~1910–1914). From 1918 to 1925, he was an editor for Die Katholischen Missionen.

Alfonsa Ferrari worked in Tibetology, Indology, and Buddhist studies. She studied at Sapienza University of Rome and Paris under Tucci, Formichi, Bloch, Renou, Bacot, and Lalou, later serving at Sapienza as Docent (1949) and Professor of Sanskrit (1951).

Alfred Bloch was an Indologist and linguist who earned his Ph.D. at the University of Basel (1933–1939). He later served at Basel as a PD (1942) and as Lehrbeauftragter für Indogermanistik and Lecturer of Hebrew (1949–1982).

Scholar of Buddhist studies, religion, and Japanology Alfred Bloom studied at Harvard under Masatoshi Nagatomi. He served as professor of religion at Oregon (1961–1970), professor at Hawaiʻi at Mānoa (1970–1986), and dean at the Institute of Buddhist Studies (1986–1994).

Alfred Chilton Pearson was a scholar in linguistics and other fields. He studied at King's College School, Highgate School, and Christ's College, Cambridge, where he was taught by John Peile from around 1879 to 1883.

Linguist and Indologist Alfred Cooper Woolner studied under Arthur Anthony Macdonell at Trinity College, Oxford. He served as Principal of Oriental College (1903), Honorary Librarian (~1902–1928), and Dean of University Instruction at the University of the Punjab (1903–1936).

Alfred Cort Haddon studied at King's College London and Christ's College, Cambridge. He held academic posts at the Royal College of Science for Ireland (1880–1901) and the University of Cambridge (1879–1880; 1900–1926), where he taught Govind Sadashiv Ghurye.
Alfred Darby was an Indologist and linguist. He studied at St Augustine's College, Canterbury, and earned a B.D. from Durham University by 1908, later holding an academic post at Rajaram College.

Alfred Edward Housman studied at King Edward's School, Bromsgrove School, and St John's College, Oxford. Working in linguistics and other fields, he held a post at University College London from around 1892 to 1911, where he taught Mortimer Wheeler.

Linguist Alfred Ernout studied at Lille, the Sorbonne, and the EPHE under Antoine Meillet. He held professorships at Lille (1913–1924) and Paris (from 1924), was directeur d’études at the EPHE (1925), and taught at the Collège de France (1944–1951).

Sinologist and philosopher Alfred Forke studied at Geneva, Berlin, Rostock, and the Seminar für Orientalische Sprachen under Carl Arendt. He taught at Berlin's Seminar for Oriental Languages (1903–1923), UC Berkeley (1914–1918), and the University of Hamburg (1923–1935).

Indologist and archaeologist Alfred Foucher studied at the École Normale Supérieure and under Sylvain Lévi at the EPHE. He served as a professor at the University of Paris (1907; 1929–1936) and directed the Délégation Archéologique Française en Afghanistan (1922–1925).

Alfred Gell studied at Trinity College, Cambridge under Edmund Leach and completed his Ph.D. at the London School of Economics. He subsequently held teaching posts at the University of Sussex (1972–1974), the Australian National University (1974–1979), and the LSE (1979–1997).

Indologist and linguist Alfred Hillebrandt studied under Adolf Friedrich Stenzler at Breslau and Martin Haug at Munich. He spent his career at the University of Breslau, where he became an extraordinary professor in 1883 and a full professor from 1887 to 1921.
